tips.title: Sonata form, with an introduction
tips.body: The movement is in **sonata form** — exposition, development, recapitulation — but it opens with a **slow introduction**, which was **unusual in piano sonatas**. Haydn used them in symphonies. The introduction then comes back in the **development** and again in the **coda**, which is the structural point examiners ask about.

tips.title: The second subject is in the wrong key
tips.body: A Classical sonata-form exposition puts the second subject in the **relative major** — here that would be **E flat major**. Beethoven starts it in **E flat minor** instead, at bar 51, and only reaches E flat major at bar 89. Naming that surprise is worth a mark on its own.

tips.title: Fortepiano is not forte-piano the instrument
tips.body: The dynamic marking **fortepiano** means **loud, then immediately soft**. The **fortepiano** was also the name of the instrument Beethoven wrote for. Say which you mean: the marking appears constantly in this movement, alongside **sforzando** — a sudden accent on one note or chord.

tips.title: Grave and Allegro, two metres
tips.body: The introduction is **Grave** — very slow — in **common time**. The main section is **Allegro di molto e con brio** — very fast and with vigour — in **alla breve** (cut time), a fast **two in the bar**. A question about tempo or metre usually wants both, and the contrast between them.

tips.title: Bar numbers, not timings
tips.body: The Pearson guide gives **bar numbers**, and so should your answers: the second subject at **bar 51**, the development at **bar 133**, the recapitulation at **bar 195**. Recordings differ in speed, so a time in minutes and seconds proves nothing; a bar number is evidence.

steps.title: Where this set work sits
steps.body:
This is the **first movement of Piano Sonata no. 8 in C minor**, known as the **Pathétique**. It belongs to the area of study **Instrumental music 1700 to 1820**, alongside Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5.

**The composer.** Ludwig van Beethoven was born in **1770** in **Bonn**, in western Germany. As a young man he moved to **Vienna**, where he became known as a **virtuoso** pianist — *virtuoso* meaning considerable skill and agility in difficult, showy music. He performed his own improvisations and compositions as well as other composers' music, mainly in the **salons** of wealthy aristocrats but also in grander concerts.

At this stage he was **beginning to go deaf**, though not yet severely enough to stop performing. It worsened rapidly, and he even contemplated suicide; in later years he composed while **totally deaf**.

**The sonata.** This was his **8th published sonata**, written between **1796 and 1799**, and dedicated to the Viennese aristocrat **Prince Karl von Lichnowsky**.

**The name.** *Pathétique* is French for **moving** or **emotional**, and it was given by the **publisher** in the first edition — not by Beethoven himself. It marked a new, passionate style.

**Where it sits in history.** Beethoven is one of the great composers of the **Classical** period, with Mozart and Haydn, both of whom he knew. He knew **Mozart's sonata in C minor, K 457**, written around fifteen years earlier, and was influenced by it — but this piece is **more revolutionary** in its extreme dynamics and unusual structure, and it shows early signs of the **Romantic** style to come.

steps.title: The instrument, and why dynamics matter
steps.body:
When Beethoven wrote this at the end of the eighteenth century, the **piano had almost completely replaced the harpsichord** as the keyboard instrument for home and concert hall — though it was still seen as a recent invention, widely used only for about twenty years, with frequent new developments in **power, tone quality and sustaining ability**.

It was often called the **fortepiano**. Whether you call it that or **pianoforte**, the name explains its popularity: ***piano*** is Italian for **soft**, ***forte*** for **loud**. Dynamics could now be changed simply by **altering the pressure of the fingers on the keys**.

**On a harpsichord that was impossible.** The mechanical action meant that on basic instruments the dynamic could not be changed at all — only by having an **extra keyboard**, or by using a lever or **coupling** mechanism.

Mozart and Haydn had begun to use dynamic markings. **Beethoven was one of the first to use all kinds of dynamic possibilities extensively**, and this sonata has frequent **crescendos**, **diminuendos** and many other performance markings.

**The sustaining pedal** was coming into use at the time, and was **sometimes worked by the knees** rather than the foot. Note carefully: the **original edition contains no pedal markings**, although Beethoven would almost certainly have used some kind of sustaining system when he played it himself.

steps.title: The slow introduction, bars 1 to 10
steps.body:
**Introductions were unusual in piano sonatas**, though Haydn's symphonies of the time often had them. This one runs from **bar 1 to bar 10** — just 10 bars — and is marked **Grave** (pronounced *grah-vay*), meaning **very slow**.

**The motif.** It opens with a distinctive **6-note motif** in **homophonic** texture. A *motif* is a short melodic idea. This one is used **throughout the introduction in different textures and keys**, and Beethoven varies it:

- sometimes the **first note is left out**, reducing it to five notes
- sometimes the **second-last note rises** to the final note instead of descending

**Other features.** The introduction contains **rapid scalic flourishes**, and ends with a **long descending chromatic scale** that leads into the Allegro.

**Key.** It is in **C minor**, modulating briefly to the **relative major, E flat**.

**Dynamics.** There is **constant dynamic contrast** here and throughout the piece, with frequent **fortepiano** (loud then immediately soft) and **sforzando** (a sudden loud accent on an individual note or chord).

**Why it matters structurally.** This introduction is not merely a preface. Four bars of it **return in the development at bar 133**, and again in the **coda at bar 295** — which is what makes the structure of this movement unusual.

steps.title: The exposition
steps.body:
The main section is marked **Allegro di molto e con brio** — **very fast and with vigour** — in **alla breve** or **cut time**, a fast **two in the bar**.

**First subject, bars 11 to 50.** The theme is in **C minor**, the **tonic**. It **rises mainly scalically through two octaves**, over a **tonic pedal in the bass**, and is marked **staccato** — detached notes.

- A **subsidiary theme** begins at **bar 27**, featuring **sforzandos** and **descending arpeggios**.
- A **transition** based on the main theme begins at **bar 35**, using **sequences**, and modulates towards the expected key of **E flat major** through **dominant preparation**.

**Second subject, bars 51 to 132.** Here is the surprise: it begins in the **unexpected key of E flat minor**, not the expected E flat major.

- The theme features a distinctive **acciaccatura** ornament and a **hand-crossing** technique, where the **right hand moves down over the left** to play four staccato notes before returning.
- It continues with a **stepwise descending phrase featuring mordents**.
- A **new theme at bar 89** arrives in the relative major, **E flat major**, with a **new broken chord texture** and a **crescendo while the hands move in contrary motion**.
- A **third theme at bar 113** makes much use of **scalic melody** and reinforces the new E flat major key. This final section can also be called a **codetta** — a short rounding-off section.

**The whole exposition is then repeated.**

steps.title: Development, recapitulation and coda
steps.body:
**Development, bars 133 to 194.** It begins with **four bars of the introduction material**, now in the **dominant key of G minor** — *a very unusual structural feature*, because a development normally works on the exposition's themes, not on an introduction.

- The Allegro then introduces the **main first subject theme in the unrelated key of E minor**.
- **Fragments of the theme are heard in the bass from bar 149.**
- **Long dominant preparation begins at bar 167**, where the dominant note **G** is played in **rapid alternating octaves in the bass as a pedal**.
- A passage of **trills** leads to a descending **monophonic quaver passage in the right hand**.

**Recapitulation, bars 195 to 294.** It repeats the music of the exposition but **alters the keys of the second subject material**. This time the second subject starts in the **subdominant, F minor**, at **bar 221**, before moving to the expected **tonic**. All three main ideas of the second subject are heard, and the recapitulation finishes with **two fortissimo diminished seventh chords**.

**Coda, bar 295 to the end.** **Four bars of the introduction**, this time **with silence on the first beat** — again a very unusual idea — lead to **12 bars of Allegro** with the first subject theme. The music ends with **fortissimo perfect cadences**, using a **dominant seventh**, in the **tonic key**.

steps.title: Tonality and harmony
steps.body:
**Tonality.**

- The key of the piece is **C minor**.
- It modulates to a number of **related keys**, including **E flat major** (the relative major) and the **subdominant, F minor**.
- It also modulates to **unrelated keys**, such as **E minor** at the beginning of the development.

**Harmony.** The writing is far more chromatic than a typical Classical sonata, and four features are named in the guide:

- Many **chromatic chords**, especially **diminished sevenths** — one occurs **half way through bar 1**.
- **Distinctive perfect cadences** at the end of the movement.
- An **interrupted cadence in the introduction, at bar 9**.
- **Circle of fifths, bars 244 to 249.**
- **Augmented sixth chords**, for example at **bars 30 and 34**.

**Why this matters.** A diminished seventh is an unstable, tense chord that can resolve in several directions, which is exactly why it suits the *pathétique* character. An interrupted cadence promises a perfect cadence and then denies it, which is why one appears in the introduction — the music will not settle until much later.

steps.title: Melody, texture, rhythm
steps.body:
**Melody.**

- The slow introduction is based on the short **six-note motif** heard at the very beginning, used as the basis for most of the introduction, **sometimes reduced to five notes**, and sometimes with the **second-last note rising instead of falling**.
- There are many **scalic passages**, such as the **descending chromatic scale** at the end of the introduction.
- The **first subject theme from bar 11** is built on an **ascending scale of the tonic key, C minor, but with a major third (E)**. Notice the distinctive **augmented second from A flat to B natural**.
- Melodic lines also include **arpeggios and broken chords**, for example at **bars 29 to 30**.
- **Ornaments** are an important feature of the second subject in particular: **acciaccaturas** at bar 53 onwards, **mordents** shortly afterwards, and **trills** just before the recapitulation.

**Texture.**

- The slow introduction has many passages of **homophonic (chordal)** writing, for example bar 1.
- The **right hand plays in octaves** later in the introduction, for example bar 5.
- A long descending **monophonic** passage in the right hand leads into the recapitulation.
- The second subject material is **melody and accompaniment** — also called **melody-dominated homophony**.
- There are examples of **two-part** writing with broken chords in the second idea of the second subject, for example **bar 93**.
- There is a brief passage **in thirds** where the trills are, **bars 181 to 187**.

**Tempo, metre and rhythm.**

- The introduction is **Grave** in **common time**; the main section is **Allegro di molto e con brio** in **alla breve**, a fast two in the bar.
- **Dotted rhythm** is an important feature, for example bar 1.
- There are some very rapid notes, including **septuplets and 1/128th notes in bar 10**.
- **Continuous quavers** are a distinctive feature of the accompaniment to the first subject.
- **Staccato crotchets** are important in the right hand of the first subject.

steps.body:
Play a recording of the movement with the table below beside you, and fill it in **as you listen**. Use **bar numbers** if you have the score; if not, write what you hear in order and match it to the sections afterwards.

**Part A.**

1. Name the tempo marking of the introduction, and of the main section.
2. How many bars is the introduction?
3. In what key does the movement begin and end?

**Part B.**

4. Listen for the moment the fast music begins. What is the marking?
5. Listen for the second subject. Does it sound major or minor when it arrives?
6. Listen for the return of the slow music. It happens **twice** after the introduction — where?

**Part C.**

7. Write the six sections of the movement in order, with their bar numbers.
8. Explain why starting the second subject in E flat minor is a surprise.
9. Choose one moment where the dynamics are extreme and describe what Beethoven does.

For question 9, name the marking — *fortepiano*, *sforzando*, *crescendo* — rather than saying "it gets loud".

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Always attach a bar number.** "The second subject is in E flat minor" is worth less than "the second subject enters in **E flat minor at bar 51**". The Pearson guide gives bars, examiners expect them, and they can be checked — a timing cannot.

**Explain why a feature is unusual, not just that it is.** The development opening on the introduction is unusual **because a development normally works on the exposition subjects**. The second subject in E flat minor is unusual **because Classical sonata form expects the relative major**. The *because* is where the marks are.

**Connect the harmony to the character.** A **diminished seventh** is unstable and can resolve several ways; an **interrupted cadence** promises resolution and withholds it. Both suit a piece the publisher called *pathétique*. That link between a technical feature and the effect is what separates the top band.

**Use the right word for the key relationship.** E flat major is the **relative major** of C minor. F minor is the **subdominant**. G minor is the **dominant**. E minor is **unrelated**. Naming the relationship shows more than naming the key.

**Distinguish the two senses of fortepiano.** The **instrument** and the **dynamic marking**. A question about the instrument wants the contrast with the harpsichord, which could not change dynamics by touch.

**Remember what the original edition does not contain.** There are **no pedal markings**, although Beethoven would have used sustaining in performance. That is the kind of precise, checkable fact a top answer includes.

**Count the returns of the introduction.** It is heard at the start, again at **bar 133** in the development, and again in the **coda at bar 295** — the third time **with silence on the first beat**. Three appearances, each different.

**Place the piece on the boundary.** Classical in form and period, with **early signs of the Romantic** in its dynamic extremes and structural freedom. Say both.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Piano Sonata no. 8 in C minor**, first movement, the **Pathétique**; area of study **Instrumental music 1700 to 1820**.
- Beethoven, born **1770** in **Bonn**, working in **Vienna** as a **virtuoso** pianist; beginning to go deaf.
- His **8th published sonata**, written **1796–1799**, dedicated to **Prince Karl von Lichnowsky**.
- *Pathétique* means **moving** or **emotional**, named by the **publisher**.
- **Classical**, with early signs of the **Romantic**; influenced by **Mozart's K 457**.
- Written for the **fortepiano**: *piano* = soft, *forte* = loud; the harpsichord could not change dynamics by touch. **No pedal markings** in the original edition.
- **Sonata form** with a **slow introduction**, which returns in the **development** and the **coda**.
- Introduction **bars 1–10**, **Grave**, **common time**, a **6-note motif**, ending with a **descending chromatic scale**.
- **Allegro di molto e con brio**, **alla breve** — a fast two in the bar.
- First subject **bar 11**, C minor, scalic rise of **two octaves** over a **tonic pedal**, staccato.
- Second subject **bar 51** in **E flat minor** — the surprise — with **acciaccatura** and **hand-crossing**; E flat major at **bar 89**; codetta at **bar 113**.
- Development **bar 133**: four bars of the introduction in **G minor**, first subject in **unrelated E minor**, dominant pedal from **bar 167**.
- Recapitulation **bar 195**; second subject in the **subdominant F minor** at **bar 221**; ends with **two fortissimo diminished sevenths**.
- Coda **bar 295**: the introduction again, **with silence on the first beat**, then **fortissimo perfect cadences** with a **dominant seventh**.
- Harmony: **diminished sevenths**, **interrupted cadence bar 9**, **augmented sixths bars 30 and 34**, **circle of fifths bars 244–249**.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the first movement of the Pathétique sonata, explaining what is unusual about it. Refer to bar numbers and keys. (8 marks)
questions.solution:
The movement is in **sonata form** — exposition, development, recapitulation and coda — but it is prefaced by a **slow introduction**, which was **unusual in a piano sonata**, though Haydn used them in symphonies.

The **introduction, bars 1 to 10**, is marked **Grave** in common time, built on a **six-note motif**, and ends with a **long descending chromatic scale**. It is in **C minor**, touching the relative major E flat.

The **exposition** begins at **bar 11** with the **first subject in C minor**, rising scalically through two octaves over a **tonic pedal**, marked staccato. A transition at bar 35 uses sequences and dominant preparation. The **second subject enters at bar 51 in E flat minor** — a surprise, because Classical sonata form expects the **relative major**. E flat major only arrives with the new broken-chord theme at **bar 89**, and a scalic **codetta** follows at **bar 113**. The whole exposition is then **repeated**.

The **development, bars 133 to 194**, is the most unusual passage. It opens not with an exposition theme but with **four bars of the slow introduction, in the dominant key of G minor**. The Allegro then presents the first subject in the **unrelated key of E minor**, with fragments in the bass from bar 149, and a long **dominant pedal** on G in rapid alternating octaves from bar 167.

The **recapitulation, bars 195 to 294**, restates the exposition but **alters the second subject keys**, beginning in the **subdominant, F minor, at bar 221** before reaching the tonic, and closing with two **fortissimo diminished seventh** chords.

The **coda from bar 295** brings the introduction back a **third** time, now **with silence on the first beat**, before 12 bars of Allegro and **fortissimo perfect cadences** with a dominant seventh in the tonic.

What makes the structure remarkable is therefore not sonata form itself but Beethoven's treatment of the introduction as **thematic material returning across the movement**, and his choice of **unexpected keys** at both appearances of the second subject.

What makes the structure remarkable is therefore not sonata form itself but Beethoven's treatment of the introduction as **thematic material returning across the movement**, and his choice of **unexpected keys** at both appearances of the second subject.

questions.prompt: Explain how Beethoven uses the resources of the fortepiano in this movement, referring to dynamics, texture and technique. (8 marks)
questions.solution:
The **fortepiano** had almost completely replaced the harpsichord by the time this sonata was written, and its central advantage is in its name: ***piano*** means soft and ***forte*** loud, and the player changes between them simply by **altering the pressure of the fingers on the keys**. On a harpsichord the **mechanical action** fixed the volume; the only way to change it was an **extra keyboard** or a **coupling** lever. Beethoven was among the first to exploit the new instrument fully.

**Dynamically**, the movement is marked by **constant contrast**. **Fortepiano** — loud then immediately soft — and **sforzando** — a sudden accent on a single note or chord — appear frequently, alongside numerous **crescendos** and **diminuendos**. The recapitulation ends with two **fortissimo** diminished sevenths and the coda with **fortissimo** perfect cadences.

**Texturally** he uses the whole instrument. The introduction is largely **homophonic and chordal**, as at bar 1, and later has the **right hand in octaves**, as at bar 5. A long descending **monophonic** passage in the right hand leads into the recapitulation. The second subject is **melody-dominated homophony**, with **two-part** writing over broken chords at bar 93 and a brief passage **in thirds** where the trills occur, bars 181 to 187.

**Technically** the writing is demanding in a way that suits a virtuoso performer. The second subject uses **hand-crossing**, the right hand moving down over the left to play four **staccato** notes before returning. **Ornaments** are prominent — **acciaccaturas** from bar 53, **mordents** shortly after, **trills** before the recapitulation. Bar 10 contains extremely rapid notes, including **septuplets and 1/128th notes**.

It is worth adding that the **original edition contains no pedal markings**, even though the sustaining pedal was coming into use — sometimes operated by the knees — and Beethoven would almost certainly have used some sustaining when playing it himself.

questions.prompt: Which statement best places the Pathétique in music history?
options: Classical in form and period, with early signs of the Romantic style
Fully Romantic, and unlike anything by Mozart or Haydn
A late Baroque work influenced by Bach
A Classical work with no forward-looking features
questions.solution: Beethoven is a great **Classical** composer alongside Mozart and Haydn, and this piece uses Classical sonata form — but its **extreme dynamics and unusual structure** show **early signs of the Romantic style to come**.

questions.prompt: Compare the way Beethoven uses key and harmony in the Pathétique first movement with what a listener would expect of a Classical sonata-form movement. Refer to specific bars. (12 marks)
questions.solution:
A listener in the 1790s would bring firm expectations to a sonata-form movement in a minor key. The **second subject** should appear in the **relative major** — for C minor, that is **E flat major** — providing contrast and brightness. The **development** should modulate, but to **closely related** keys. The **recapitulation** should restate both subjects in the **tonic**, resolving the tonal argument. Harmony should be largely **diatonic and functional**, with chromatic chords used sparingly for colour.

Beethoven meets almost none of these expectations straightforwardly.

**The second subject enters at bar 51 in E flat minor**, not E flat major. The key is right; the **mode is not**. The expected relative major arrives only with the new broken-chord theme at **bar 89**, so the contrast the listener expects is **delayed** by nearly forty bars and darkened when it does come.

**The recapitulation** departs further. Rather than placing the second subject in the tonic at once, Beethoven begins it in the **subdominant, F minor, at bar 221**, reaching the tonic only afterwards. The resolution is postponed a second time.

**The development** goes beyond closely related keys altogether. It opens with four bars of the **slow introduction in the dominant, G minor**, and then states the first subject in the **unrelated key of E minor** — a relationship no Classical listener would predict.

**Harmonically** the movement is markedly more **chromatic** than the norm. **Diminished sevenths** appear from the outset, one **half way through bar 1**; **augmented sixth chords** occur at **bars 30 and 34**; a **circle of fifths** drives bars **244 to 249**. The introduction even contains an **interrupted cadence at bar 9**, promising a perfect cadence and withholding it.

The cumulative effect is a movement that constantly **defers resolution**. Each device — the minor-mode second subject, the subdominant recapitulation, the unrelated development key, the unstable diminished sevenths, the interrupted cadence — postpones the stability the form promises. That is precisely what makes the piece *pathétique*, the publisher's word for moving or emotional, and it is why the sonata is heard as Classical in form but already **Romantic in feeling**.

examTechnique.body:
Give a **bar number** with every observation — the guide does, and a bar can be checked while a timing cannot. Name **key relationships**, not just keys: E flat major is the **relative major**, F minor the **subdominant**, E minor **unrelated**.

For the "unusual" questions, say **why**: a development normally works on the exposition subjects, and Classical form expects the second subject in the relative major. Link harmony to character — diminished sevenths and an interrupted cadence suit a piece called *pathétique*.
examinerErrors: Giving a timing instead of a bar number.
Saying the second subject is in E flat major in the exposition.
Calling the development ordinary because it modulates.
Confusing the instrument fortepiano with the dynamic marking.
Saying the original edition has pedal markings.
Naming a key without naming its relationship to the tonic.
Forgetting that the exposition is repeated.
Treating the piece as fully Romantic rather than Classical with Romantic signs.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer attaches a bar number to every claim and names the key relationship as well as the key. It explains what is unusual and **why** it is unusual — the development opening on introduction material rather than a subject, the second subject in E flat minor where the relative major was expected, the recapitulation delaying the tonic by starting in F minor. It links the chromatic harmony to the expressive character, counts the three returns of the introduction including the silence on the first beat in the coda, and places the work as Classical in form with early signs of the Romantic.
